key_terms.meaning: F(x, y) = P(X ≤ x and Y ≤ y), a function on the plane that is non-decreasing in each argument and tends to 0 along the far left and far bottom edges and to 1 at (+∞, +∞)
p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y) for discrete X, Y; it is non-negative and sums to 1 over all pairs
f(x, y) ≥ 0 with double integral over the whole plane equal to 1, and P((X, Y) ∈ A) = ∬_A f(x, y) dx dy
The law of one variable alone: p_X(x) = Σ_y p(x, y) for discrete variables, f_X(x) = ∫ f(x, y) dy for continuous ones
f_{Y|X}(y|x) = f(x, y) / f_X(x), the law of Y once X = x is known (defined where f_X(x) > 0)
E[Y | X = x] = Σ_y y·p_{Y|X}(y|x) or ∫ y·f_{Y|X}(y|x) dy; a function of x, not a number
X and Y are independent when F(x, y) = F_X(x)·F_Y(y) for every pair, equivalently p(x, y) = p_X(x)·p_Y(y) or f(x, y) = f_X(x)·f_Y(y)
Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E[XY] − μ_X μ_Y, in units of X times units of Y
ρ = Cov(X, Y) / (σ_X σ_Y), a pure number with −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1
Cov(X, Y) = 0, which means E[XY] = E[X]·E[Y]; independence implies this but not the reverse in general
P(|Z − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² for k > 0, giving a bound on spread with no assumption on the shape of the distribution
For i.i.d. X₁, X₂, … with finite mean μ, the sample mean X̄_n = (X₁ + … + X_n)/n satisfies P(|X̄_n − μ| ≥ ε) → 0 for every fixed ε > 0
X̄_n → μ with probability 1, a stronger statement than the weak law because it holds for the whole sequence at once
Z_n = (S_n − nμ) / (σ√n) with S_n = X₁ + … + X_n; it has mean 0 and variance 1 for every n
For i.i.d. variables with mean μ and finite variance σ², Z_n → standard normal in distribution, so P(Z_n ≤ z) → Φ(z)
The ±0.5 adjustment used when a discrete sum is approximated by a normal, e.g. P(S_n ≤ 30) becomes P(S_n ≤ 30.5)
μ = E[X] = (E[X₁], …, E[X_d])ᵗ for a random vector X = (X₁, …, X_d)ᵗ
Σ with entries Σ_ij = Cov(X_i, X_j); symmetric and positive semi-definite, with variances on the diagonal
X is multivariate normal when every linear combination aᵗX is a normal variable; the density is f(x) = (2π)^(−d/2)|Σ|^(−1/2) exp(−½ (x − μ)ᵗ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ))
For multivariate normal X with covariance Σ, the transform Y = Σ^(−1/2)(X − μ) gives independent standard normal components

takeaways: A pair of random variables is described completely by one joint function on the plane; marginals and conditionals are just sums, integrals and ratios of that one function.
Two variables are independent exactly when the joint is the product of the marginals at every point, not merely when their covariance is zero.
Covariance measures only linear co-movement; it changes if you change units, so correlation is the unit-free version.
Independence gives E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] and forces zero covariance, but zero covariance forces independence only in the jointly normal case.
The weak law says the sample mean converges in probability to the population mean; Chebyshev's inequality gives the standard proof.
The central limit theorem adds a rate and a shape: the standardized sum settles onto a standard normal curve, so probabilities can be read from Φ tables.
The normal approximation to a binomial or Poisson sum needs a continuity correction when the underlying variable is discrete.
A multivariate normal is fixed entirely by its mean vector and covariance matrix, and its parts are independent exactly when that matrix is diagonal.
bank_note: Long answers here link one derivation (joint to marginal to conditional, or a moment-generating-function proof of the weak law and the central limit theorem) with a numerical part on a given joint density or a normal approximation.

bank.q: Define the joint CDF of two random variables X and Y and state its main properties. Show how the marginal CDFs F_X and F_Y are recovered from F(x, y), and how P(a < X ≤ b, c < Y ≤ d) is written using F.
outline: F(x, y) = P(X ≤ x, Y ≤ y)
Values in [0, 1], non-decreasing in each argument, right-continuous
F_X(x) = F(x, ∞) and F_Y(y) = F(∞, y)
Rectangle probability by double difference F(b, d) − F(a, d) − F(b, c) + F(a, c)

bank.q: The joint pmf of discrete X and Y is given in a table. Build the marginal pmfs, test whether X and Y are independent, and compute P(X + Y ≤ 3) and E[X | Y = 1].
outline: Row sums and column sums give the marginals; each must total 1
Check p(x, y) = p_X(x) p_Y(y) for every cell, not just one
Sum the joint over the pairs satisfying X + Y ≤ 3
Conditional pmf p_{X|Y}(x|1) = p(x, 1)/p_Y(1), then average x

bank.q: Define Cov(X, Y). Prove Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y], show that independent variables are uncorrelated, and give an example of uncorrelated variables that are not independent.
outline: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)]
Expand the product and use linearity of expectation
Independence gives E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], so Cov = 0
Counter-example: X symmetric about 0 and Y = X² has Cov = 0 but Y is fully determined by X
Bilinearity: Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac·Cov(X, Y)

bank.q: State Chebyshev's inequality and use it to prove the weak law of large numbers for i.i.d. variables with mean μ and finite variance σ².
outline: Statement: P(|Z − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k², equivalently P(|Z − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ²/ε²
Mean and variance of X̄_n: μ and σ²/n
Apply the inequality to X̄_n with ε fixed
Bound σ²/(nε²) → 0 as n → ∞
Conclusion: convergence in probability of X̄_n to μ

bank.q: The joint pdf of X and Y is f(x, y) = c(x + y) on 0 < x < 1, 0 < y < 1 and zero elsewhere. Find c, both marginals, the conditional density of Y given X = x, and P(X + Y < 1).
outline: Normalize: double integral of c(x + y) equals 1, giving c
f_X(x) = ∫ f(x, y) dy and f_Y(y) = ∫ f(x, y) dx
f_{Y|X}(y|x) = f(x, y)/f_X(x) with the correct support
P(X + Y < 1) by integrating over the triangle x + y < 1

bank.q: For a given joint density f(x, y) with support 0 < y < x < 1, find E[Y | X = x] and verify the law of total expectation E[Y] = E[E[Y | X]].
outline: Find f_X(x) by integrating out y over 0 < y < x
Form f_{Y|X}(y|x) and integrate y times it
Obtain a function of x, for example x/2
Average that function over the density of X
Check the result equals E[Y] computed from the joint directly

bank.q: A fair coin is tossed 400 times. Use the central limit theorem with a continuity correction to estimate the probability of getting between 185 and 215 heads inclusive, and compare with what Chebyshev's inequality guarantees.
outline: S_n is binomial with n = 400, p = 0.5, mean 200, variance 100
Standardize with continuity correction: 184.5 and 215.5
Chebyshev gives only a weak lower bound using σ = 10 and k = 1.5
Comment on the sharpness of the CLT answer versus the bound

bank.q: The pair (X, Y) is bivariate normal with μ_X = 1, μ_Y = 2, σ_X = 2, σ_Y = 3 and ρ = 0.5. Write the joint density, find the conditional distribution of Y given X = 3, and compute P(Y > 4 | X = 3).
outline: Cov(X, Y) = ρσ_Xσ_Y = 3
Write the exponent using the quadratic form with the 2 × 2 covariance matrix
Conditional mean μ_Y + ρ(σ_Y/σ_X)(x − μ_X)
Conditional variance σ_Y²(1 − ρ²) = 27/4
Standardize and read from the normal table

bank.q: Contrast the weak and strong laws of large numbers. Explain what each says about the whole sequence of sample means, why the strong law implies the weak law, and why neither one gives the shape of the fluctuation of X̄_n around μ.
outline: Weak: for each fixed ε, P(|X̄_n − μ| ≥ ε) → 0
Strong: P(lim X̄_n = μ) = 1, a statement about the whole path
Strong implies weak; the converse fails
Conditions: finite mean for the strong law (i.i.d. case), finite variance for the Chebyshev proof of the weak law
Fluctuation size is of order σ/√n and its shape is the subject of the CLT

bank.q: State the central limit theorem for i.i.d. variables and prove it using moment generating functions. State clearly where the proof uses the existence of the MGF and give a distribution for which the CLT fails.
outline: Statement in terms of the standardized sum Z_n and Φ
MGF of Z_n written as a product of n identical MGFs
Taylor expand the MGF of (X − μ)/σ near 0 to second order
Take logarithms and use the limit (1 + a/n)ⁿ → eᵃ
Identify the limit as e^(z²/2), the standard normal MGF
Heavy-tailed failure: the Cauchy distribution has no finite variance and its mean of n terms is again Cauchy

bank.q: For jointly normal X and Y, prove that ρ = 0 implies independence, and explain why the same statement is false for general distributions. Extend the argument to a random vector with a diagonal covariance matrix.
outline: Write the bivariate normal density with ρ = 0
The exponent splits into a sum of an x-term and a y-term
The density factorizes into the product of the two marginals
General counter-example: X uniform on [−1, 1] and Y = X²
For a d-dimensional normal, diagonal Σ makes Σ⁻¹ diagonal and the density a product of d normal densities

bank.q: Let X be multivariate normal with mean vector μ and covariance matrix Σ, and let Y = AX + b for a constant matrix A and vector b. Derive the mean vector and covariance matrix of Y, and use the result to show how to decorrelate X.
outline: E[Y] = Aμ + b by linearity
Cov(Y) = AΣAᵗ derived from the definition
Linear combinations of Y are linear combinations of X, hence normal
Choose A = Σ^(−1/2) to get identity covariance
The components of Y are then independent standard normal variables
Caveat: A must be invertible or use the symmetric square root

bank.q: A quality-control engineer wants a bound on the chance that the average weight of 100 packets differs from the target by more than 5 g. Compare the answers given by Chebyshev's inequality and by the central limit theorem, and say when each is the right tool.
outline: Model the weights as i.i.d. with mean μ and standard deviation σ
Chebyshev: P(|X̄ − μ| ≥ 5) ≤ σ²/(100 × 25), valid for any distribution
CLT: approximate the same probability by 2(1 − Φ(5√100/σ))
Chebyshev is conservative but assumption-free; CLT is sharp but needs n large
With n = 100 and a light-tailed weight distribution the CLT answer is usually preferred

glossary.def: The complete probability law of a pair (X, Y), giving the probability of every region of the plane.
The function p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y) for discrete variables, summing to 1 over all pairs.
A non-negative function f(x, y) whose double integral over any region gives the probability that (X, Y) falls in that region.
F(x, y) = P(X ≤ x, Y ≤ y), defined for all pairs of real numbers.
The distribution of one variable obtained by summing or integrating the joint over all values of the other.
The distribution of Y after X = x is fixed, equal to the joint divided by the marginal of X.
E[Y | X = x], the mean of the conditional distribution of Y at a fixed value x of X.
The property that the joint distribution factorizes into the product of the marginals everywhere.
E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)], the average product of the two deviations from their means.
Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y), a scale-free measure of linear association lying between −1 and 1.
Having zero covariance, so that E[XY] = E[X]E[Y].
The result that the sample mean of i.i.d. observations approaches the population mean as n grows.
Z_n → Z in probability when P(|Z_n − Z| ≥ ε) → 0 for every fixed ε > 0.
Z_n → Z with probability 1, meaning the set of outcomes where the sequence fails to converge has probability 0.
The result that the standardized sum of i.i.d. variables with finite variance converges in distribution to the standard normal.
Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation so the new variable has mean 0 and variance 1.
A half-unit adjustment that improves a normal approximation to a discrete probability.
The vector whose entries are the means of the components of a random vector.
The symmetric matrix whose (i, j) entry is Cov(X_i, X_j) and whose diagonal holds the variances.
A symmetric matrix M with aᵗMa ≥ 0 for every vector a; every covariance matrix has this property.
A random vector whose every linear combination of components is normally distributed.
The two-dimensional case of the multivariate normal, fixed by two means, two standard deviations and one correlation.
The matrix of correlations between the components of a random vector, obtained by scaling the covariance matrix.
The set of points where a joint pmf or pdf is positive, which must be stated when writing conditionals.
